title: Vitamin D Hypersensitivity as a Potential Trigger for Worsening Vascular Calcification: A Hypothesis
content: Observational studies have consistently associated low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D₃] levels with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, but large randomized trials and Mendelian randomization studies have failed to demonstrate a causal relationship. We propose that this paradox is partly explained by the considerable interindividual variability in vitamin D (VD) response. In individuals with VD hypersensitivity (VDHY)— due to CYP24A1 mutations, ectopic 1α-hydroxylase activity in granulomatous diseases, or other disorders of 1,25(OH)₂D₃ production or catabolism—tissue 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D [1,25(OH)₂D₃] accumulates even with moderate sunlight exposure or conventional supplementation. We hypothesize that this local excess inhibits parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) in vascular smooth muscle cells, removing a key inhibitor of osteogenic transdifferentiation and thereby promoting vascular calcification. This mechanistic framework integrates vascular biology, endocrinology, and genetics and may explain why traditional monitoring of serum 25(OH)D₃ levels fails to measure cardiovascular risk. We propose that the development of clinical vitamin D response assays is necessary to reliably assess vitamin D requirements.
